9701-2.1.1.motivate: An atom is too light for everyday mass units to be convenient. A common reference lets us compare atomic masses directly.
9701-2.1.1.establish: The unified atomic mass unit, $u$, is defined as one twelfth of the mass of one carbon-12 atom. Thus one carbon-12 atom has a mass of exactly $12u$. The definition selects a particular isotope, carbon-12, rather than an average carbon atom. Actual atomic masses may be expressed in $u$; relative masses are ratios to $u$ and have no units.
9701-2.1.1.connect: This fixed carbon-12 reference is the denominator in the definitions of relative isotopic, atomic, molecular and formula mass.
9701-2.1.1.note:
- One unified atomic mass unit is one twelfth of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.
- One carbon-12 atom has mass exactly $12u$.
- Relative masses are unitless ratios to this reference.
9701-2.1.1.self_explain: Why does one carbon-12 atom have a mass of exactly $12u$?

9701-2.1.2.motivate: A symbol, isotope label, molecule and ionic formula refer to different entities. Naming the mass correctly tells the examiner which entity you mean.
9701-2.1.2.establish: Relative isotopic mass is the mass of one atom of a specified isotope relative to one twelfth of the mass of one carbon-12 atom. Relative atomic mass, $A_r$, is the weighted mean mass of an atom of an element relative to that reference; isotope abundances determine the weighting. Relative molecular mass, $M_r$, is the mass of one molecule relative to the reference. Relative formula mass is the mass of one formula unit relative to the reference, used for ionic compounds without discrete molecules. Add the constituent $A_r$ values, respecting subscripts, to calculate molecular or formula mass. These are relative ratios without units.
9701-2.1.2.connect: The choice of entity determines the term: an element has $A_r$, a named isotope has relative isotopic mass, a molecule has $M_r$, and an ionic formula unit has relative formula mass.
9701-2.1.2.note:
- Relative isotopic mass concerns one atom of one isotope.
- $A_r$ is the abundance-weighted mean for atoms of an element.
- $M_r$ concerns one molecule; relative formula mass concerns one formula unit.
- Each is measured relative to one twelfth of a carbon-12 atom's mass and has no unit.
9701-2.1.2.self_explain: Why is 35.5 appropriate for chlorine's $A_r$ but not for the relative isotopic mass of chlorine-35?
